analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators set safety rules for guns like other consumer products.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2001 with a single cosponsor, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have applied consumer-product-style regulation to firearms and ammunition for the first time. The Treasury Secretary could set design and performance safety rules, order recalls or refunds of dangerous guns, inspect factories and dealer records, and fine or prosecute violators. It also required manufacturers to test and certify products, required labels tracing the maker and model, and directed the government to collect and publish data on gun deaths and injuries.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to gun violence and defective firearms. The bill would have required safety testing and certification of guns before sale, let anyone petition for a recall of a dangerous model, given shooting victims a right to sue for damages with possible attorney's fees, and created a public record of gun-related deaths and injuries that families, researchers, and regulators currently cannot see.

how_it_helps.text: Directed the Treasury Secretary to write regulations covering the design, manufacture, and performance of firearm products as reasonably necessary to reduce or prevent unreasonable risk of injury [S2][S3].

Authorized the Secretary to order recalls, repairs, replacements, or refunds of firearm products found to pose an unreasonable risk, be defective, or violate regulations, and to ban outright any product that remains unreasonably dangerous [S2][S3].

Made it unlawful to sell a gun that had not been tested and certified as conforming to the safety regulations, and required labels identifying the manufacturer, importer, model, and manufacture date [S2][S3].
Gave any injured person a private right to sue for damages, including consequential damages and attorney's fees, and let any interested person sue to enforce the Act [S3].

Required the government to collect and publish data on the circumstances of firearm deaths and injuries, keep production and sales figures by model and serial number, and report annually to Congress on injuries, enforcement, and industry meetings [S2][S3].
Allowed any person to petition the Secretary to issue, amend, or repeal a regulation or to require a recall, with a decision and stated reasons due within 120 days [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers, who would face mandatory safety testing and certification, labeling requirements, factory and record inspections, fines up to $10,000 per product ($20,000 if willful), possible criminal penalties, recall and refund costs, and increased exposure to civil lawsuits. Some compliance costs could be passed on to gun buyers through higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill grants very broad authority to a single cabinet secretary, including power to prohibit manufacture of any product deemed unreasonably risky and to bar 'stockpiling' sales above a pre-regulation base rate, which opponents viewed as a way to effectively restrict types of firearms without new legislation [S3].
It requires the government to keep production and sales figures by model, caliber, and serial number, which gun rights advocates have long characterized as a step toward a firearms registry [S3].

Private enforcement suits available to 'any interested person,' combined with per-product fines, could generate substantial litigation and compliance costs for small dealers, including pawnbrokers, and some of that cost would reach consumers as higher prices [S3].

A good-faith objection is that firearms, unlike toasters or car seats, are constitutionally protected products, so treating them as ordinary consumer goods is seen by many as an inappropriate regulatory frame even where specific safety rules are sensible.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea mirrors rules that already apply to nearly every other physical product Americans buy: test it, label it, recall it if it is defective, and keep records. The potential public benefit is real but indirect, since most gun deaths come from intentional use that product-safety rules address only at the margins, through defective designs, untraceable sales channels, and missing data. The costs fall on a concentrated industry and are partly passed to buyers, and the breadth of the Secretary's power and the serial-number data collection are legitimate concerns that would have needed tightening. On balance this is a consumer-safety bill whose design would have benefited from the committee process it never received.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in February 2001, and the committee never acted on it before that Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Torricelli introduced the Firearms Safety and Consumer Protection Act of 2001 on February 14, 2001 [S1][S5].
One Senate Democrat cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, where no further action was recorded before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].
The bill never reached the Senate floor and received no vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers came out ahead: they avoided mandatory safety testing and certification, labeling, government inspection of factories and records, recall and refund orders, per-violation fines, and a new private right to sue.

for.name: Sen. Robert Torricelli
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup, hearing, or vote on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators, both Democrats, are recorded as supporting the bill, and no senator is recorded as opposing it, so no partisan breakdown of a vote exists.

industries.note: The bill would have subjected gun and ammunition makers to the same safety-testing, certification, labeling, recall, and inspection regime as other consumer products, with fines and a new private right to sue. Their interest was in keeping a largely unregulated product category unregulated, which runs against the bill's public-safety purpose.

The bill defined dealers to include pawnbrokers and would have required them to label products, maintain and open records for government inspection, and comply with any safety orders, with liability for violations.
